label: September 18–20 · Opening-week practice
connection: We have practised conversation, Discovery activities and Werewolf. Place value is part of our September plan; try the maths review only if it is familiar. Other choices below are optional general practice, not a claim that every subject has already been taught.

activities.subject: Math
activities.title: What is each digit worth?
activities.context: September place-value review · choose familiar work
activities.example: 2,406 = 2,000 + 400 + 6. The zero holds the tens place.
steps: Write 6,307 in expanded form. What does the zero tell you?
Write 4,052 in expanded form. What is the value of the 5?
If decimals are familiar, compare 0.5 and 0.05. Draw or explain why.
activities.check: 6,307 = 6,000 + 300 + 7; zero tens. 4,052 = 4,000 + 50 + 2; the 5 is worth 50. 0.5 > 0.05 because five tenths is greater than five hundredths.
activities.extension: Choose a larger number. Change one digit and explain how much its value changes.

activities.subject: Language Arts
activities.title: Read, notice and explain
activities.context: Connects to reading and listening routines
activities.example: Try: ‘I think the character is worried because they keep checking the door.’ For nonfiction: ‘The main idea is … One detail is …’
steps: Read or listen to a short part of a book you choose.
Tell, draw or write one important event or idea.
Point to one detail that helped you understand it.
activities.check: Can someone follow your explanation? Can you point to the detail in the text? A spoken answer counts.

activities.subject: Language Arts
activities.title: Tell a tiny mystery
activities.context: Connects to storytelling and reasoning in Werewolf
activities.example: A library book disappears. A bookmark is on the sofa and a book-shaped lump is under a cushion. The reader finds it there.
steps: Invent a missing-object mystery with a beginning, problem and ending.
Tell it in about one minute. Include two clues.
Ask which clue helped your listener; retell one part more clearly. You can practise alone or with a toy.
activities.check: Does the ending fit both clues? Did you keep imagined details separate from real events?

activities.subject: Social Studies
activities.title: Make a game fairer
activities.context: Connects to games and our classroom community
activities.example: Allow a practice round before scoring so a beginner can learn the rules.
steps: Choose a familiar game. Explain one rule and whom it helps.
Imagine a new player cannot join in easily. Suggest one change.
Explain how your change helps people participate.
activities.check: Name who benefits and explain why. Could your change create a different problem? Revise it if needed.

activities.subject: Science
activities.title: Notice before you guess
activities.context: General observation practice · no new science unit assigned
activities.example: ‘The leaf has a brown edge’ is an observation. ‘It may have dried out’ is a possible explanation.
steps: Choose a safe everyday object, such as a spoon or leaf.
Draw it and write three things you can directly observe.
Write one question and one possible explanation. Label the explanation ‘I think …’.
activities.check: Can you separate what you observed from what you think caused it? Do not taste unknown objects or plants.

activities.subject: French
activities.title: Use words you already know
activities.context: Review only · use familiar classroom words
activities.example: If familiar: bonjour = hello; merci = thank you; au revoir = goodbye.
steps: Choose three French words or phrases you have already learned.
Say each one and match it to a picture or meaning.
Cover your notes and try again. If none are familiar yet, skip this choice.
activities.check: Can you match each phrase to its meaning without looking? Check classroom notes; ask at school about pronunciation.

activities.subject: Arts Education
activities.title: Draw the same object twice
activities.example: A mug handle may appear on the side in one view and be hidden in the other.
steps: Draw a safe everyday object from the front.
Turn it or move your seat and draw it from another angle.
Circle one detail that changed and one that stayed the same.
activities.check: Can someone tell the drawings show different views? Explain one choice of line or shape.

activities.subject: ADST
activities.title: Build, test and improve
activities.example: Fold a sheet into a tent. If it tips, try a wider base.
steps: Use one sheet of scrap paper to make a freestanding name card. Keep it at home.
Test whether it stands for ten seconds.
Change one fold and test again. Draw or describe what improved.
activities.check: What did you change? Did the second version stand more steadily? An unsuccessful test still gives useful information.

activities.subject: Physical and Health Education
activities.title: Move in a way that works for you
activities.context: Connects to active play and shared rules
activities.example: Try three favourite movements with pauses between them.
steps: Choose a walk, dance, stretch or comfortable seated movement.
Choose a safe space and a pace that feels manageable.
Notice how you feel before and after.
activities.check: Describe how your body felt and one choice that helped you move safely. There is no speed or distance target.

activities.subject: Career Education
activities.title: Prepare for tomorrow
activities.example: ‘I can pack my book. I need help finding the form.’
steps: Check your planner or the reminder you were given.
Choose one useful task: pack a book, organize supplies or put a form where an adult will see it.
Name one thing you can do independently and one thing you need help with.
activities.check: Can you find the item you need? Choose one small next step; do not share private family information.
